
The model is a set of self-contained C++ headers. **They use no R and no Rcpp**,
depend only on Boost and the header-only parts of `odelia`, and compile and run
with no R installed at all. That is a guarantee rather than an accident, and
`.github/workflows/cpp-tests.yml` enforces it by building the whole C++ suite on
runners with no R on them.

This vignette contains no runnable R. It documents the other half of the package,
which R users never see and `plant` uses exclusively.

## The two umbrella headers, and why the extension matters

```
#include <phylloptim.hpp>    // the model. Plain C++, no R, no Rcpp.
#include <phylloptim.h>      // the R binding layer. Pulls in Rcpp.
```

If you are embedding the model, you want `.hpp`. The `.h` file exists
because `RcppR6` hardwires both that name and `<phylloptim/RcppR6_pre.hpp>`, so
the R-facing umbrella had to take it and the model's had to move. A file
extension carries the whole one-way dependency rule, which is more weight than an
extension should bear, hence the banner at the top of each.

The rule: `src/` and `R/` include *downward* into `inst/include/`, never the
reverse. Nothing reachable from `<phylloptim.hpp>` includes Rcpp. The CMake
install rules encode the same split, shipping `*.hpp` and **excluding**
`phylloptim.h` and the generated `RcppR6_*.hpp`, so a non-R consumer is never
handed a header they cannot compile.

## Building

Two dependencies, both header-only: Boost (root finders and the incomplete
gamma function) and `odelia` (the supplied-derivative nodes and vendored XAD). `odelia` is distributed as an R package
but the headers used here are plain C++, so a git checkout is enough.

```sh
git clone https://github.com/traitecoevo/odelia
cmake -B build -DPHYLLOPTIM_ODELIA_INCLUDE_DIR=$PWD/odelia/inst/include
cmake --build build
ctest --test-dir build          # the C++ suite, including the golden file
cmake --install build --prefix /usr/local
```

```cmake
find_package(phylloptim REQUIRED)
target_link_libraries(my_program PRIVATE phylloptim::phylloptim)
```

An INTERFACE target: headers, an include path and `cxx_std_20`, nothing to link.
`add_subdirectory()` works too if you would rather vendor it.

**Build with optimisation on if you intend to compare against the golden
file.** Measured on macOS/arm64, `-O1`, `-O2` and `-O3` all reproduce
`tests/cpp/golden/operating_points.tsv` bit-for-bit and `-O0` does not, missing by
about 13 ULP because it declines to contract `a*b + c` into an FMA. A debug build
failing `test_golden` by ~1e-15 has found nothing.

## A solve

```cpp
#include <phylloptim.hpp>
#include <cstdio>

int main() {
  phylloptim::Leaf l;                    // default Eucalyptus saligna traits
  // A Leaf defaults to TF24_floor on the leaf route over one soil potential;
  // a root network and the collar solve, as plant runs them, are seated.
  l.set_supply_multilayer();
  l.set_model(phylloptim::Leaf::CostCurve::TF24, /*collar_route=*/true);

  std::vector<double> psi_soil{2.0};     // positive magnitudes, MPa
  std::vector<double> soil_depth{1.0};   // m

  // The per-layer root RESISTANCES, per unit leaf area. If you have root carbon
  // instead, this is the architecture model that maps one to the other -- but it
  // is a helper you call, not something the solve does (#33). Supply the
  // resistances directly if that is what you have.
  const phylloptim::RootNetwork roots = phylloptim::root_network_from_carbon(
      /*root carbon per m2 LEAF*/ {20.0},
      phylloptim::layer_thicknesses(soil_depth), /*beta_R_H*/ 3.4e2,
      /*beta_R_V*/ 9.4e3);

  l.set_physiology(roots, /*PPFD*/ 900, psi_soil, soil_depth,
                   /*kmax*/ 3.14e-5, /*atm_vpd*/ 2.0, /*ca*/ 40.0,
                   /*leaf_temp*/ 25.0, /*atm_o2_kpa*/ 21.0,
                   /*atm_kpa*/ 101.3);
  l.find_root_collar_psi();

  std::printf("A = %.6f, gc = %.6f, psi_leaf = %.6f\n",
              l.assim_colimited_, l.stom_cond_CO2_, l.opt_psi_leaf_);
  return 0;
}
```

Every water potential is a **positive magnitude in MPa**, and that is asserted
rather than documented: a negative `psi_soil` is an error, not a sign convention
the model quietly accepts.

## Trait gradients from C++

`<phylloptim/gradient.hpp>`, reached from the umbrella header, gives the trait gradient at a solved point with no R anywhere, as one forward pass of the derivative surface carrying every parameter, and batches it over observations.

```cpp
#include <phylloptim.hpp>
namespace g = phylloptim::gradient;

g::Drivers d;                                  // one observation's drivers
d.root_network = roots; d.PPFD = 900; d.psi_soil = {2.0};
d.soil_depth = {1.0}; d.atm_vpd = 2.0; d.ca = 40.0;
d.leaf_temp = 25.0; d.atm_o2_kpa = 21.0; d.atm_kpa = 101.3;

double theta[g::n_theta] = {/* 16 traits, then kmax, resistance, the three model-owned slots, the damage inputs */};
const int pars[1] = {0};                       // g::par_names()[0] == "vcmax_25"

phylloptim::Leaf l;
l.set_supply_multilayer();
g::Settings s;                                 // the Leaf's defaults, unless set:
s.model = {phylloptim::Leaf::CostCurve::TF24, g::Route::Collar};
const std::vector<g::Result> out =
  g::batch(l, theta, 1, {d, d}, /*single=*/false, pars, 1, s);
// out[i].grad[k * g::n_outputs + j] is d(output j)/d(pars[k])
// out[i].status is Interior / Pinned / NoGradient / Error
```

To evaluate at a collar potential you are carrying rather than one to be solved
for, which is the case a model that *tracks* the optimum has, pass `psi`, one per
observation, and optionally an `n × npars` column-major `dpsi_dtheta`:

```cpp
const double psi[2] = {2.7, 2.8};              // positive magnitudes, MPa
const std::vector<g::Result> out =
  g::batch(l, theta, 1, {d, d}, /*single=*/false, pars, 1, s,
           psi, /*dpsi_dtheta=*/nullptr);      // null here means ZERO...
// out[i].status is now Prescribed or Refused
// out[i].M / out[i].H are the coefficients of ds/dt = k(M + H s)
```

A null `dpsi_dtheta` means zero: the collar was imposed, so it moves only as you
say it does. For one observation, use `g::at()` with a `g::Prescribed`.

`theta` is `g::n_theta` = **35** doubles: the sixteen traits in `set_traits`'
argument order, then `leaf_specific_conductance_max`, the single-potential path's
`resistance`, the three model-owned slots `CF77_lambda_`, `TF24_floor_lambda_o`
and `LeastCost_beta`, and the fourteen inputs of the thermal-damage layer that
reach the solve. `g::par_names()` is that order and every position has a name
(`g::par_vcmax_25`, `g::par_R_d_25`, `g::par_kmax`, ...); `pars` holds positions
into it. R indexes these positions, so reordering the enumeration silently
differentiates the wrong parameter. `phylloptim::n_leaf_pars` is **37**, two longer:
the pack the kernels read also holds `par_PPFD` and `par_NIR`, seated per
observation from the drivers and never fitted. Size `theta` by `n_theta`; read it out to `n_leaf_pars` and
you run past its end.

**Count the initialiser against `g::n_theta` rather than against this
paragraph.** A short aggregate initialiser is legal C++ and zero-fills the rest, so
a `theta` written from a stale count shifts every parameter after the gap and drops
the last off the end, with no diagnostic at all. That has happened: a 16-entry list
under what was then an 18-element array put `kmax` in a trait's slot, and the only
symptom was `dA/dvcmax = nan`. The package's own CI consumer carries a
`static_assert(g::n_theta == 35)` beside its list for exactly this reason; copy it.

Three things the free function gives you that a hand-rolled loop would not:

* **the classification.** The solve records what kind of point it found,
  interior or held by a bound, and the pass places the decision variable
  accordingly: by the implicit function theorem at an interior optimum, on the
  bound at a pinned one. Where the optimum sits on a bound, `-M/H` is wrong by
  orders of magnitude and fails silently; `status` says which it was.
* **one pass for every parameter.** The pass runs at `g::n_theta + 1` lanes, one
  per slot and one for the decision variable, so its cost does not depend on
  `pars`.
* **per-row status rather than an exception**, so a proposal that reaches an
  unsolvable point costs that row and not the batch.

**It is every trait gradient the package gives**: `leaf_gradient()` and
`leaf_gradient_batch()` both call it. `Settings::model` names the curve and the
route, the `Leaf`'s default (TF24_floor on the leaf route) unless set. `tests/testthat/test-gradient-referee.R`
checks it against a difference of the solve for every curve on both routes, and
`tests/cpp/test_leaf_surface.cpp` checks the surface itself at every kind of
point.

The surface is public, if you want to compose something else; plant does, to
read the operating point's rows at its own scalar type:

| piece | what it is |
|---|---|
| `supply_draw_at<S>(collar, supply)` | the supply's draw at a collar, on any scalar |
| `operating_collar<K, S>(draw, pars, H, &held)` | the decision variable placed from the kind the solve recorded |
| `physical_outputs_at<K, S>(x, draw, pars, &held)` | A, gc, psi_leaf and profit at that placement |
| `profit_curvature_at_collar<K>()` | `H`, the curvature the implicit function theorem divides by |
| `dprofit_droot_collar_psi(psi, &feasible)` | dprofit/dψ at a given collar potential, at double |

**Pass the `feasible` flag.** `dprofit_droot_collar_psi` returns `0.0` on its
shut-down and reversed-gradient exits, and a bare zero is indistinguishable from a
stationary point, so a root-find looking for `dprofit == 0` would converge onto a
shut-down state and report it as the optimum. The optional `bool*` second
argument is how the two are told apart.

`vignette("derivative-surface")` documents the surface: what each kind places,
and what each scalar type is for.

## What is fast, and what is not

`tests/cpp/bench_gradient.cpp` times the gradient beside a central difference of
the whole solve, both in C++, at one interior point (TF24 on the collar route,
one layer), less the seat and solve every arm pays:

| arm | cost |
|---|---|
| the gradient, any number of parameters | about 9 µs |
| a difference of the solve | about 5 µs a parameter, and tens where it rebuilds a vulnerability table (`stem_c`, `root_c`) |

So the pass costs about two parameters' worth of differencing, and then nothing
more: from three parameters up it is the cheaper of the two, and it is exact.

That is also what an R caller gets from `leaf_gradient_batch()`: the pass runs
in C++ over every observation, so the boundary is crossed once per call rather
than once per observation.

**Constructing a `Leaf` from R is the largest single cost in the R layer**, and
most of it is R-side object construction rather than the vulnerability tables.
From C++ that cost is the tables alone. Reuse the object either way. The measured
figures for all of these are in the README's
[Performance from R](https://github.com/traitecoevo/phylloptim#performance-from-r),
the one place they are kept current.

## The golden file is the contract

`tests/cpp/golden/operating_points.tsv` records 672 operating points at full
precision and is compared **bit-exactly**. It is what makes a large refactor of
this code checkable rather than hopeful, and any change that moves it is expected
to say what moved and by how much.

It is bit-exact on the platform that generated it (macOS/arm64) and compared with
per-field tolerances elsewhere, because libm's `exp`/`pow` are not
bit-reproducible across platforms. The fields split into two classes three orders
apart: `profit` is the maximum itself and well conditioned; everything else is
evaluated at the *argmax* of a flat maximum and so sqrt-amplified. **If you need a
portable check of the solve, check `profit`.**
